Nursing Resume Example: Write a Nurse Resume That Passes the ATS in 2026

Nursing resumes face a double gate: the hospital's applicant tracking system (ATS) and a nurse manager who skims each application in seconds. Generic duty lists — "provided patient care," "assisted physicians" — fail at both. The ATS ranks you low on keyword match, and the manager sees no evidence of what you can handle on a unit.

What gets shortlisted is proof: an active license up front, named certifications (BLS, ACLS), clinical settings described with patient ratios and unit types, the EMR systems you chart in, and outcomes with numbers. Below: a complete annotated example, plus the ATS rules for nursing hiring.

Quick answer: A nursing resume should include: active RN license and state, BLS/ACLS certifications, clinical experience with patient ratios and unit types, EMR proficiency (e.g., Epic, Cerner), measurable outcomes (fall reductions, code responses), and keywords mirrored from the posting. Hospital ATS systems scan for these exact credentials first — generic duty lists without numbers get ranked down.

Key Takeaways

  • Put licenses and certifications FIRST — RN license (state, status), BLS, ACLS. Hospital ATS systems filter on these before reading anything else.
  • Name your clinical environment precisely: unit type, patient ratios (e.g., 1:4 med-surg), bed count, and EMR (e.g., Epic, Cerner).
  • Quantify outcomes: fall-rate reductions, code blue responses, HCAHPS scores, precepting results.
  • Mirror the posting's exact specialty terms — "Telemetry," "Med-Surg," and "Step-down" are different ATS keywords.
  • Keep formatting ATS-clean: single column, standard headings, no graphics, no text boxes, no creative section titles.

Nursing Resume Example (Annotated)

YOUR NAME, RN
City, ST | (555) 555-0100 | youremail@email.com
linkedin.com/in/yourname

LICENSES & CERTIFICATIONS
Registered Nurse (RN) — [State], active license (expires 2027)
Basic Life Support (BLS) — American Heart Association (expires 2026)
Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) — American Heart Association (expires 2026)

PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
Registered Nurse with 5 years in medical-surgical and telemetry nursing, managing 1:4–1:5 ratios on 32-bed units. Proficient in Epic charting, IV therapy, and wound care. Two Daisy Award nominations for patient satisfaction scores above 95%.

Why it works: years, specialties, ratios, unit size, EMR, one outcome metric — every claim verifiable.

CLINICAL EXPERIENCE

Registered Nurse — Med-Surg / Telemetry | 2021 – Present
• Manage 1:4–1:5 patient ratios on a 32-bed telemetry unit, administering medications and titrating IV drips per protocol
• Reduced patient fall rate 30% by implementing an hourly rounding checklist adopted unit-wide
• Respond to 10+ rapid response and code blue events monthly as part of the rapid response team
• Precept 6 new graduate nurses through 12-week orientation; all retained past their first year

Why it works: ratios, unit size, specific interventions, one improvement metric, code volume, preceptor leadership, EMR named literally.

Registered Nurse — Medical-Surgical | 2019 – 2021
• Cared for 1:5–1:6 patient assignments on a 28-bed med-surg unit
• Maintained patient satisfaction scores above the 90th percentile on HCAHPS surveys
• Coordinated discharge planning with case management for 15+ patients weekly

EDUCATION
Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) — [University] | 2019

CLINICAL SKILLS
Epic, Cerner | IV insertion and phlebotomy | wound care | telemetry monitoring | medication administration | patient education | discharge planning | triage

What Nursing Hiring Managers and Hospital ATS Scan For

The Jobscan 2026 ATS Usage Report puts ATS usage at 97.4% of Fortune 500 companies — and hospital systems are among the heaviest users, since one nursing posting can draw hundreds of applicants. The ATS filters before any human reads your resume, scoring on exact credential and keyword matches.

Here's what both the software and the nurse manager look for, in priority order:

  1. License and certifications. Active RN/LPN license, BLS, ACLS, specialty certs (PALS, TNCC, CCRN). If the posting requires ACLS and your resume never says "ACLS," you can be filtered out regardless of experience.
  2. Clinical setting. Unit type (ICU, ER, telemetry, med-surg, L&D), patient ratios, bed count, trauma level. "1:4 telemetry, 32-bed unit" says what you've handled; "provided patient care" says nothing.
  3. Systems and skills. Epic, Cerner, Meditech — recruiters search these terms literally. IV therapy, wound care, triage, telemetry monitoring, discharge planning.
  4. Outcomes with numbers. Fall-rate reductions, code blue volume, HCAHPS scores, precepting results, charting compliance — the same proof-over-adjectives principle in our customer service resume example.
  5. Keywords from the posting. Mirror exact terms. If the posting says "step-down unit," write "step-down unit," not "progressive care." The parser matches text, not intent.

New-Grad vs. Experienced Nurse Resume Structure

New graduates

  • Lead with education and clinical rotations: BSN/ADN, graduation date, NCLEX-RN pass status, then rotations — unit type, facility size, hours, skills practiced. Example: "Med-Surg rotation, 120 hours — 1:3–1:4 assignments with preceptor; IV insertion, wound care, Epic documentation."
  • Certifications carry extra weight. BLS is expected; ACLS (and PALS for pediatrics) before you apply stands out.
  • Translate adjacent experience. CNA, patient care tech, EMT, or medical assistant work counts — quantify it. See our guide to writing a resume with no experience.

Experienced nurses (2+ years)

  • Lead with a 3-line summary (years, specialties, ratios, one metric), then reverse-chronological clinical experience.
  • Condense rotations to one line under education, or drop them after 5+ years.
  • Show progression: charge nurse duties, precepting, committee work, quality-improvement projects.
  • Changing specialties? Front-load transferable skills (titrated drips, telemetry, rapid response) in the summary so the ATS and manager see the bridge.

The Exact Sections of a Nursing Resume

1. Licenses & Certifications

Always first for nursing. Format: credential, issuing body, state, status, expiry year. Spell out the full term on first use with the abbreviation in parentheses — "Basic Life Support (BLS)" — so the parser matches both forms. Never list an expired certification as current.

2. Professional Summary (3 lines max)

Years + specialties + ratios/unit size + one metric + target. New grads: lead with education instead (e.g., "New graduate RN, NCLEX-RN passed 2026, seeking med-surg residency; 720 clinical hours across med-surg, telemetry, ICU").

3. Clinical Experience

Reverse-chronological: title, unit/specialty, dates. Every bullet should carry at least one of: patient ratio, unit size, a specific intervention, or a measured outcome. "Responsible for patient assessments" gets ignored; "Head-to-toe assessments for 1:4 telemetry assignments, documented in Epic with 98% audit compliance" gets interviews.

4. Education

Degree, school, graduation year. New grads can add honors and relevant coursework; experienced nurses keep it to one line.

5. Clinical Skills

A scannable list for the ATS keyword scan — name things literally: EMR systems (e.g., Epic, Cerner), procedures (IV insertion, phlebotomy, wound care), competencies (triage, discharge planning, patient education). Our registered nurse resume guide has specialty-specific keyword lists.

ATS Formatting Rules for Nursing Resumes

  • Single column, always. Two-column templates scramble parsing order — your license can end up attributed to the wrong section. Pick a single-column ATS-friendly template.
  • Standard headings: Summary, Licenses & Certifications, Clinical Experience, Education, Clinical Skills. "My Nursing Journey" is invisible to the parser.
  • No tables, text boxes, or graphics. Skill bars, icons, and text boxes are dropped or misread by most parsers. Plain text only.
  • Contact info in the body, not the header/footer. Many parsers skip headers and footers — if your phone number lives there, it may never be extracted.
  • Standard fonts, 10–12pt. Arial, Calibri, Georgia, Times New Roman.
  • File type: PDF unless the posting asks for .docx. Never Pages, image, or scanned files.
  • Length: one page for new grads; two pages max for experienced nurses. Cut oldest roles first, not the metrics.
  • Verify before you apply: run your resume through Cvyon's free ATS grader against the actual posting to catch parsing errors and keyword gaps.

7 ATS Mistakes Nurses Make

  1. Burying the license below the fold. The ATS filters on license and certifications first. On page two, they may never be read.
  2. Duty lists with no ratios or units. "Provided direct patient care" matches nothing. "1:4 telemetry, 32-bed unit" matches the posting's requirements.
  3. Abbreviations without expansion. Write "Basic Life Support (BLS)" and "Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS)" at least once — some systems index the full term, others the abbreviation.
  4. Creative section headings. "Clinical Journey" and "Where I've Healed" don't map to the parser's expected sections. Use the standard five.
  5. Two-column "modern" templates. They look sharp and parse terribly — content order scrambles, and certifications can vanish from the extracted text.
  6. Missing the posting's exact specialty term. The posting says "progressive care" and you wrote "step-down" everywhere — keyword score drops. Mirror their words.
  7. Stale certifications. Listing ACLS with a 2023 expiry as current reads as careless. Update the resume the day you recertify.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a nursing resume?

Active RN license with state and status; BLS/ACLS and specialty certifications; a summary with years, specialties, and patient ratios; clinical experience with unit types, bed counts, and measured outcomes; education; and a clinical skills section naming EMR systems (e.g., Epic, Cerner). Every bullet should carry a number — ratios, volumes, or outcome metrics.

How do I write a nursing resume with no experience?

Lead with education, NCLEX-RN pass status, and a Clinical Rotations section: unit type, hours, and skills practiced per rotation (e.g., "Telemetry rotation, 120 hours — 1:3–1:4 assignments, IV insertion, Epic documentation"). Add BLS/ACLS, and translate CNA, EMT, or patient-care-tech work into quantified bullets. New grads are hired on credentials and clinical exposure, not job titles.

What certifications should a nurse put on a resume?

BLS and ACLS from the American Heart Association, plus specialty certs matching your target: PALS for pediatrics, TNCC for trauma/ER, CCRN for critical care. List the issuing body and expiry year — and only list current certifications. An expired cert presented as current damages credibility.

How long should a nursing resume be?

One page for new graduates and nurses under 5 years' experience; two pages maximum for experienced nurses. When trimming, cut older roles and redundant bullets — never the license section, certifications, or your strongest metrics.

Should I put my RN license number on my resume?

State and active status are enough (e.g., "Registered Nurse (RN) — [State], active"). The number is verified during credentialing, so it isn't required at the resume stage. Never list an expired license without marking its status honestly.

Do nursing resumes need to be ATS-friendly?

Yes — hospital systems receive hundreds of applications per posting, so ATS screening is near-universal in nursing hiring. Use a single-column layout, standard headings, licenses first, exact certification names, and keywords mirrored from the posting. Verify with Cvyon's free ATS grader before you apply.
